item.title: The 'myth' of Western-style democracy is losing its appeal even in the West: Global Times editorial
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-04 00:09:00
Demonstrators face off with law enforcement officers during a protest in Paris, France, on October 17, 2026. Photo: Xinhua The most fundamental and significant standard for evaluating whether a democracy is good is whether it can consistently provide the populace with stable livelihoods, clear expectations, and hopeful prospects. A poll released by the Pew Research Center this year shows that public satisfaction with how democracy works in their own countries is declining dramatically. Dissatisfaction rate stands at 69 percent in France, 68 percent in Spain, 62 percent in Italy, 47 percent in Poland and 69 percent in the US. In fact, sustained tracking by several other prominent Western polling organizations, including Ipsos and Gallup, points to the same trend: Dissatisfaction with the functioning of democracy in Western countries is evolving from isolated discontent into a widespread public sentiment. This dissatisfaction is not merely reflected in polling figures; it is also visible on the streets across the Western world. Each Western country has its own set of problems. Some are plagued by frequent changes in political leadership, while others remain mired in the challenges of immigrant integration. Some are grappling with the painful effects of the energy transition and the steady decline of traditional industries, while others are struggling to contain increasingly intense social divisions. Yet polling data reveal a common thread running through public sentiment: More and more people no longer believe their governments genuinely represent the interests of ordinary citizens, or that existing political systems are capable of delivering meaningful change. Calls for fighting corruption, strengthening accountability, making public policies more responsive and ensuring that ordinary people's voices are genuinely heard have become shared demands across party lines and social classes in Western societies. Many once believed that voting was the entirety of democracy: As long as electoral procedures were followed, the outcome was legitimate and the popular will would naturally find its way into policymaking. But a growing number of people in Western countries are now realizing that voting is more like a periodic ritual. Making a choice once every few years does not guarantee that people will continue to have a say in public affairs in their daily lives between elections. According to a relevant OECD survey released this year, 68 percent of respondents believe that voting in an election has a significant or moderate influence on what government does, but only 31 percent are confident that people like them have a say in what government does. When people seeking to have their concerns addressed find that their votes often fail to translate into policy responses, their confidence in democracy naturally erodes in the face of reality. Current discussions among some Western elites about "what has gone wrong with democracy" often veer toward two one-sided explanations: either blaming all the problems on agitation by populists or attributing public dissatisfaction to a "loss of patience" with democracy. Both explanations evade a basic fact: The dissatisfaction with democracy in Western countries does not stem from misunderstanding, but from the failure of existing democratic institutions to respond effectively to public demands and meet societal needs. Following the end of the Cold War, Western countries experienced a period of relative social stability. At that time, the legitimacy of Western democracy did not derive from the so-called "end of history," but rested on the West's dominant advantages across multiple fields. As globalization accelerated, capital mobility increased, and industrial production was restructured, Western governments found their ability to redistribute wealth increasingly constrained by systemic pressures. Meanwhile, institutional corruption has increasingly permeated political processes, further exposing the inherent flaws of Western democratic systems. At its core, the dissatisfaction among Western populations is not a denial of democratic values, but rather a profound disappointment with the practice of democracy in the West. Some political parties in the West are increasingly leaning their policymaking toward capital interests, while the livelihood issues of ordinary people are being set aside. Electoral politics is gradually deteriorating into a power struggle between different elite factions, with partisan conflicts, veto politics, and policy flip-flops becoming the norm. The gap between political promises and reality continues to widen. The discontent from the grassroots is continuously questioning the practical adaptability of Western democratic systems, sowing further uncertainty for the future trajectory of Western politics. For most countries, the truly beneficial insight from the Western reflection on "what has gone wrong with democracy" is that there has never been a one-size-fits-all institutional form, nor is there a democratic model that can operate independently from its local soil and the genuine needs of its people. If votes are long treated as the entirety of democracy, if party interests are placed above the public good, and if slogans replace actual governance, then no matter how glossy the institutional facade, it will ultimately be discarded amid the repeated disappointments of the populace. The most fundamental and significant standard for evaluating whether a democracy is good is whether it can consistently provide the populace with stable livelihoods, clear expectations, and hopeful prospects. Unfortunately, some Western politicians and media continue to use democracy as a political instrument for export, seeking to arbitrarily draw ideological dividing lines, form blocs and provoke ideological confrontation on the international stage. This approach not only fails to truly respond to the demands of their own citizens but also exacerbates the disconnection between democracy and reality. As a result, the credibility of Western democracy continues to erode under the dual pressures of domestic livelihood crises and external hegemonic actions, ultimately leading to a trust crisis both at home and abroad.

item.title: Chinese FM urges Philippine side to rein in relevant individuals, saying bilateral relations face malicious interference at present
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-03 23:50:00
Photo: IC Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi urged the Philippine side to rein in relevant individuals and send a rational and unified message on its China policy, in a phone conversation on Tuesday with Philippine Foreign Affairs Secretary Ma. Theresa Lazaro. Lazaro said the Philippines remains committed to its one-China policy, and is willing to resolve maritime and other issues with China through dialogue and consultation. China-Philippines relations are facing malicious interference at present, said Wang, Xinhua News Agency reported. Wang, also a member of the Political Bureau of the Communist Party of China Central Committee, said that a few Philippine politicians, out of political prejudice and self-interest, have repeatedly attacked and smeared China, noting that such deeds are irrational and intolerable, according to Xinhua. These Philippine politicians have crossed China's red lines, politicized normal economic, trade and people-to-people exchanges, and infringed upon the legitimate rights and interests of Chinese personnel and institutions in the Philippines, Wang said, noting that such actions also undermined the Philippines' international image, according to a readout released by Chinese Ministry of Foreign Affairs. Wang urged the Philippine side to rein in relevant individuals and send a rational and unified message on its China policy. China's resolve to safeguard its sovereignty and territorial integrity and achieve national reunification remains unwavering. The Philippines should fully implement its one-China policy and exercise caution in its words and actions on maritime-related issues, Wang said, per release. Lazaro said the Philippines attaches great importance to its relations with China and hopes to develop stable and predictable bilateral ties. At a time when countries around the world are facing challenges in areas such as the economy and energy, communication between the Philippines and China would help manage differences, improve bilateral relations, and promote regional peace and stability, Lazaro said, according to the release. The Philippines remains committed to its one-China policy, and this position will not change, and it is also willing to resolve maritime and other issues with China through dialogue and consultations, Lazaro added. The two sides reached a basic consensus on improving and developing bilateral ties, agreeing to maintain diplomatic dialogue, oppose malicious provocations, and responsibly manage differences and expand shared interests, according to the release. item.title: Once Japan acquires nuclear weapons, it will surely bite the hand that feeds it
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-03 23:36:00
Protesters hold a banner during a rally in Tokyo, Japan, on November 21, 2025, after Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi criticized the country's traditional policy against nuclear weapons. Photo: VCG Just as Tokyo shows signs of breaking through its "Three Non-Nuclear Principles," some individuals have "conveniently" offered up a bad idea. According to Japanese media reports on Tuesday, some experts in Washington, including a US Navy official, have suggested that Tokyo "should consider acquiring nuclear submarines," with the aim of "enabling the Japan Self-Defense Forces to deter China more effectively." However, these American "experts" are nothing but Washington's "liability." Since the Sanae Takaichi administration took office, certain Japanese politicians have become obsessed with "acquiring nuclear‑powered submarines." Japan's Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi has repeatedly and publicly advocated for the introduction of nuclear-powered submarines. In their narrative, nuclear‑powered submarines represent nothing more than an upgrade in propulsion and do not equate to carrying nuclear weapons - a word game they hope will allow them to pursue their agenda. However, the fuel cycle, spent fuel reprocessing, and nuclear material controls for nuclear-powered submarines substantially overlap with pathways for developing nuclear weapons. Japan already stockpiles large quantities of separated plutonium and has well-established reserves of nuclear material, reactor-technology expertise and delivery-platform foundations. Should Tokyo achieve the technical and political breakthrough of "introducing nuclear-powered submarines," no insurmountable technical gap would stand in the way of it later developing its own nuclear warheads. "Buy the submarines first, then acquire nuclear-weapon capability" is the roadmap quietly plotted by Japan's right-wing forces. The US is aware of these risks, yet it has long turned a blind eye. Some US politicians harbor opportunistic calculations regarding Tokyo: They want to arm Japan as their forward‑edge spearhead in East Asia and make Japan bear more of the costs of confrontation. They imagine they hold the reins and can keep this "proxy tool" firmly in check to prevent it from turning on its master. This mind-set is steeped in short‑sighted arrogance. In essence, it gambles with the postwar international order and the non‑proliferation regime, allowing the dangerous "Pandora's box" to be slowly opened for the sake of short-term geopolitical gains. Washington fantasizes that "limited rearmament of Japan" will serve its own strategy, but it underestimates the tenacity of Japan's right‑wing forces to shake off constraints. After Japan's defeat in World War II, segments of its right‑wing have relied on the US security umbrella while harboring deep‑seated resentment and frustration over the "humiliation of being bombed." Meanwhile, tens of thousands of US troops stationed in Japan serve both as a platform for US power projection and as shackles on Japan. Japan's current willingness to dance to Washington's tune stems from its insufficient strength for full independence; it needs US acquiescence to loosen restrictions. Such compliance is tactical pretense for the time being, not permanent submission. It's obvious that if Japan crosses the bottom line and truly acquires nuclear‑deterrence capacity, it will never resign itself to being a US "outpost" forever. Should the US continue to indulge Japan in challenging the "Three Non-Nuclear Principles" and allow nuclear‑related capabilities to take root on Japanese soil, it will eventually reap what it sows. If Japan possesses nuclear weapons, it will surely bite the hand that feeds it.

item.title: China to maintain capital market stability, boost long-term investment: CSRC official
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-03 23:23:00
The building of the China Securities Regulatory Commission in Beijing. Photo: VCG China's securities regulator pledged on Tuesday to maintain capital market stability and attract more long-term investment, as authorities seek to strengthen the market's ability to withstand external risks. Li Chao, vice chairperson of the China Securities Regulatory Commission (CSRC), made the remarks at the Global Financial Leaders' Investment Summit in Hong Kong on Tuesday, according to the CSRC's official news release platform. Li said that the CSRC had stepped up market monitoring and strengthened mechanisms to maintain stability in response to multiple unexpected external risks this year. The regulator will also improve policies to encourage long-term investment, deepen reforms of public mutual funds and steadily increase both the scale and proportion of investments by social security funds, pension funds and insurers, Li said. The remarks come as China continues to encourage more long-term institutional capital to enter the stock market, with recent figures showing increased investment by major institutions. Social security funds, pension funds and insurers made combined net purchases of more than 600 billion yuan ($89.94 billion) in A-shares in the first three quarters of this year, while the market value of their tradable A-share holdings was up 12.5 percent from the end of 2025, according to official data released on September 10. China's public mutual fund industry generated 1.74 trillion yuan in profits for investors in the first half of 2026, according to the CSRC. The latest remarks follow a pledge by CSRC Chairperson Wu Qing at the Financial Street Forum in Beijing on October 19 to improve long-term performance assessment mechanisms, expand investment channels for institutional funds and further reform the mutual fund industry. On market stability, Wu called for closer monitoring of risks at home and abroad, particularly those involving leveraged products linked to individual A-shares traded overseas. He also encouraged eligible listed companies to step up share buybacks and shareholding increases to better reward investors. The measures are aimed at encouraging longer investment horizons and providing a more stable source of capital for the stock market. Greater participation by pension funds, insurers and other institutional investors could also help reduce short-term volatility and improve the market's ability to support businesses and the broader economy, industry observers noted.

item.title: GT Voice: Can India's manufacturing sector avoid competition with China?
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-03 23:18:00
India China Illustration: Chen Xia/Global Times Can India become a global manufacturing powerhouse while keeping its distance from the world's largest free trade agreement, simply to avoid competition from China? As debate over India's participation in the pact resurfaces, this question is becoming harder to avoid. Critics of the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership (RCEP) in India worry that joining the pact could expose Indian industries to Chinese goods without adequate tariff protection. Yet an interview published by The Indian Express on Monday presented a different perspective. Alan Bollard, former governor of the Reserve Bank of New Zealand, suggested that India should reconsider joining the pact, noting that membership could help the country tap into the supply chains that have made China so competitive. China is among the members of the RCEP, whose economies account for about 30 percent of global GDP, population and trade. Studies estimate that the agreement could add hundreds of billions of dollars to regional income and create millions of jobs by 2030. Whether India moves to join the RCEP is ultimately its own decision. But as the country seeks to strengthen its manufacturing base and expand its presence in overseas markets, broadening its network of free trade agreements can bring clear economic benefits. One such benefit is access to markets. The RCEP brings together dynamic economies in the Asia-Pacific, including China and South Korea, offering exporters easier access to a broad regional market. At a time when rising protectionism is making access to some developed economies more difficult, the pact offers considerable economic value to countries seeking to diversify their export destinations and tap into Asia's growing market opportunities. Another benefit that is easy to overlook is participation in regional supply chains. Consider a hypothetical example: wool imported from Australia and New Zealand could be processed into fabric in China, then sent to India, where it is made into garments for export to Japan and South Korea. The RCEP could help lower trade costs along this cross-border production chain, making it easier for businesses to organize production across several economies. India's imports of fabric from China would serve as inputs for higher-value garment exports, allowing the country to capture more value through manufacturing and create jobs. The question is not simply how much India imports from China, but how much it can gain by taking part in regional production networks. This offers a more productive path than remaining outside them. As technology advances, supply chains in the Asia-Pacific region are becoming more sophisticated, specialized and interconnected. The more efficient these networks become, the higher the cost of remaining outside them. Bollard's remarks offer a useful perspective: part of China's manufacturing competitiveness stems from its effective use of supply chains across Southeast Asia and South Korea. For other economies, participating in these networks can also strengthen their own manufacturing capabilities. Whether or not India seeks to join the RCEP, the direction of its efforts is likely to be much the same: finding more export opportunities in Asia-Pacific markets and becoming more deeply integrated into the region's production networks, including those linked to China. For a country seeking to expand its manufacturing base and reach more overseas markets, participation in these networks is part of the efforts to build a globally competitive manufacturing sector. Deeper integration also comes with greater competitive pressure. Greater integration will expose Indian manufacturers to more competition, not only from Chinese products but also from goods made in other RCEP economies. This may create short-term pressure for some industries. But slowing international integration to avoid competition would carry costs of its own. The answer to competitive pressure is not to retreat from regional production networks, but to build stronger capabilities through greater participation in them. Protecting industries from competition cannot substitute for making them more competitive. India's commitment to developing its manufacturing sector and expanding its global reach is clear. Whether or not it joins the RCEP, closer integration with regional supply chains, including those linked to China, will remain an important part of that journey. The RCEP could offer India a faster route to its destination. The question is whether India is ready to get on board.

item.title: UK agency alleges China AI cyberattack threat; expert views move to keep attack edge, deny deterrence
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-03 22:58:00
Photo: VCG The UK's security agency claimed in an annual review that Britain would face a ransomware attack involving AI-powered malware by 2028, with "China best placed to launch AI-powered cyberattacks on Britain." A Chinese industry expert said that UK agency's true intent is to retain its AI cyber-offensive capacity while barring other nations from developing deterrent countermeasures. The annual report, released on Tuesday, was published by the UK's National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC), part of the GCHQ spy agency. It claimed AI will probably enable a ransomware attack against critical national infrastructure [CNI] between now and 2028. The UK's definition of CNI covers a range of facilities and services across sectors including energy, transport, defense, food, health and finance, the Guardian reported on Tuesday. Yet the annual report groundlessly alleged that countries including China "will start using AI routinely in cyber-attacks," the Guardian reported. The Independent report also claimed that "Chinese cyber activity is the most sophisticated and sustained cyber challenge facing the UK." Xiao Xinguang, chief software architect at Chinese cybersecurity company Antiy, said that the UK's mudslinging against China is merely grandstanding. "Professionals are well aware that it is Western countries, not China, that have spared no effort in advancing the weaponization of super intelligent AI," Xiao told the Global Times on Tuesday. The Financial Times reported in June that Anthropic is helping the US National Security Agency deploy its powerful Mythos AI model for offensive cyber operations, embedding engineers inside the agency. It remains unclear whether Anthropic's engineers are assisting the NSA in active operations. However, one person close to the situation said Mythos would be useful for infiltrating the networks of nations such as China or Iran, the report said. The UK's AI Security Institute disclosed that an AI agent was caught creating fake online identities to gain unauthorized access to secure systems during tests of models from OpenAI and Anthropic which revealed a series of new breaches, Reuters reported in August. The institute said agents powered by Anthropic's Mythos 5 and OpenAI's GPT-5.6-Sol engaged in unauthorized actions during security evaluations the government organization conducted to assess the models' capabilities, per the report. Xiao emphasized that it is Western institutions themselves that first identified these capabilities, yet they subsequently slung mud at China and other countries, a stance that is logically incoherent. "Their objective is precisely to preserve Western countries' capacity to launch AI attacks against other nations at any time, while denying countries that are targeted and threatened by them the right to build their own deterrent and countermeasure capabilities," Xiao added. This is not the first time that the UK has stoked hype over alleged Chinese cyberattacks. Media reported that in December, 2025 that the UK government announced sanctions on two China-based companies, alleging that they carried out cyberattacks against the UK and its allies and that their activities are linked to the Chinese government. In response, Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said that China stands against hacking and fights such activities in accordance with the law. "We firmly oppose spreading disinformation out of political agenda. China strongly deplores and firmly rejects the UK's political manipulation under the pretext of cybersecurity, and has lodged serious protests with the UK side both in Beijing and London," Guo added. Xiao said that in recent years, a small number of British politicians and agencies have echoed Washington's narrative and backed its push to let private firms conduct state-sponsored cyber strikes, seeking to broaden the scope of permissible cyber offensive actions.

item.title: China champions open AI co-op at Wuzhen Summit, calls for opposition to 'digital iron curtains'
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-03 22:17:00
The 2026 World Internet Conference Wuzhen Summit in Wuzhen, East China's Zhejiang Province opens on November 3, 2026. About 1,800 participants, including government officials, representatives of international organizations, experts and scholars, attended the opening ceremony. Photo: VCG China will respect the legitimate cybersecurity concerns of all other countries and work together with them to address security challenges, while opposing the creation of a "digital iron curtain," Chinese Premier Li Qiang said on Tuesday. Li made the remarks in a keynote speech delivered at the opening ceremony of the 2026 World Internet Conference Wuzhen Summit in Wuzhen, East China's Zhejiang Province, on Tuesday morning, the Xinhua News Agency reported. Calling for joint efforts to build a community with a shared future in cyberspace, Li said China will continue to pursue innovation through openness, promote technology transfer and knowledge sharing, and work with other countries to foster an open, inclusive and dynamic digital innovation ecosystem. The remarks came as government officials, technology executives, experts and other representatives from around the world gathered at the summit, which places artificial intelligence (AI) and open-source cooperation at the center of discussions. Several international participants at the WIC, which is running from Monday to Thursday, shared with the Global Times that they were impressed by China's advances in AI and digital infrastructure, while calling for greater international cooperation to ensure that emerging technologies benefit more countries and communities. The WIC's theme of open source and shared benefits reflects the summit's focus on the opportunities and challenges arising from the rapid development of AI, including technological innovation, security governance and international cooperation, Chinese industry analysts said. Global AI cooperation This year's summit features an "AI Wuzhen Dialogue," bringing together executives from leading global technology companies and open-source AI model developers, as well as AI scientists, to discuss the development of a global open-source AI ecosystem. There are 27 sub-forums covering a wide range of topics, including cyberspace cooperation under the Global Governance Initiative, theories and policies in the digital intelligence era, robotics and embodied intelligence. The summit has also attracted broad international participation in its technology and innovation programs. The collection of outstanding cases related to building a community with a shared future in cyberspace received more than 360 submissions from over 80 countries and regions, including 22 who are participating for the first time, according to WIC's website. Eleven cases were ultimately selected. Meanwhile, the WIC Awards for Pioneering Science and Technology attracted more than 430 technological achievements from 43 countries and regions. International submissions increased by 21 percent from the previous year, and 20 projects received awards, China News Service reported. International participants said at the WIC on Tuesday that the gathering provided an opportunity to learn about China's technological advances and explore new areas of cooperation. This was the first time Debora Comparin, co-chair for TIDA (Trust and Identity for Humans and Agentic AI) at the International Telecommunication Union has participated in the summit. She told the Global Times that she was particularly interested in China's AI ecosystem and its progress in agentic AI. "I'm looking forward to learning more about China's AI ecosystem and its companies, especially in my field, agentic AI," Comparin said. "I think China is very advanced in AI, including agentic AI. Its advantages are linked to its supply chain and value chain. China has capabilities ranging from chip manufacturing to model training, which puts it in a fairly unique position," Comparin said. Terry Sweetser, chair of the APNIC Routing Security Special Interest Group, who is visiting China for the first time, said he was impressed by the country's modern infrastructure and the scale of the conference. "Scale is a major advantage. China can bring people, resources and expertise together very quickly to tackle a problem," Sweetser told the Global Times. Sweetser highlighted China's advances in internet infrastructure and routing security, citing the adoption of Resource Public Key Infrastructure and the large-scale deployment of telecommunications infrastructure. Ousman Bajinka, senior lecturer at the University of The Gambia, told the Global Times that the summit is taking place at an important moment in technological development. "This is the right event at the right time," said Bajinka, noting that AI and the internet could jointly advance sectors ranging from agriculture and food production to medicine. Bajinka also said that other countries could benefit from China's technological advances and learn from its approach to development. Returning to the World Internet Conference Wuzhen Summit for the 11th time, John Hoffman, chairman and director of GSMA Ltd, highlighted the growing importance of connectivity and openness as the world moves from the internet of things to the internet of agents. The summit's technological showcases have attracted much coverage from foreign media. The Emirates News Agency reported on Monday that the Light of Internet Expo, a flagship event of the Wuzhen Summit, featured more than 1,000 cutting-edge technology products from 671 companies across 54 countries and regions. Openness, shared benefits As AI advances rapidly, ensuring that its benefits reach people worldwide rather than widen the digital divide has become an important topic at this year's Wuzhen Summit. At a regular press conference on Tuesday, Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning stressed that the ultimate purpose of internet development must be to promote people's all-round development, with greater emphasis on a people-centered value orientation. "Internet-related technologies should enhance people's capabilities, expand their choices, affirm human worth, and improve their well-being, rather than make people subordinate to technology, still less allow technology to exacerbate divisions in human development," Mao said. The remarks were in response to a question about the 2026 World Internet Conference Wuzhen Summit and China's views on risks in the AI era, including the abuse of technology, the digital divide and the overstretched concept of security. Mao said China will continue to pursue open innovation, promote technology transfer and knowledge sharing, and work with all to build an open, inclusive and dynamic global ecosystem for digital innovation. China will also respect the legitimate cybersecurity concerns of all countries, work with all to confront security challenges, and oppose erecting "digital iron curtains." This emphasis on openness was echoed by international participants at the summit, who highlighted the potential for cooperation on open-source technologies, common standards and practical applications of AI, even amid technological competition. Constructive cooperation between China and the US is essential for the global development of AI, particularly in open source and standardization, Comparin said, noting that "China and the US are both leading countries in AI, and absolutely need constructive cooperation." Lilan Dayananda, a social-tech entrepreneur from Sri Lanka attending the summit, also highlighted the potential for cooperation between China and developing economies. He said Sri Lanka had well-trained software engineers, creating opportunities for Chinese companies to employ local developers, while Chinese software and AI solutions could be applied in Sri Lanka. Dayananda stressed that technological competition and international cooperation are not mutually exclusive. "I like the phrase 'positive competition.' Competition is important because it helps prevent monopolies in technology," the Sri Lankan businessman said. Discussions at the Wuzhen Summit underscore the growing importance of ensuring that advances in AI translate into broader development opportunities, rather than deepening existing technological divides, Xiang Ligang, a veteran industry analyst, told the Global Times. China's rapid advances in AI, particularly its expanding open-source ecosystem, are helping lower technological barriers and create new opportunities for developing countries, Xiang said. "China's emphasis on openness, technology sharing and international cooperation reflects its commitment to making AI development more inclusive, rather than allowing its benefits to be concentrated in a handful of countries or companies," Xiang said.

item.title: China-Russia military ties advance with significant progress in high-level exchanges and joint military exercises: China's CMC vice chairman
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-03 19:01:00
China Russia Photo: Xinhua Zhang Shengmin, vice chairman of the Central Military Commission (CMC) met with visiting Russian Defense Minister Andrei Belousov at the Diaoyutai State Guesthouse in Beijing on Tuesday, China’s Ministry of National Defense (MND) announced on Tuesday. Zhang said that this year marks the 30th anniversary of the establishment of the China-Russia strategic partnership of coordination and the 25th anniversary of the signing of the China-Russia Treaty of Good-Neighborliness and Friendly Cooperation. Under the strategic guidance of the two heads of state, China-Russia relations have entered a new stage of more substantive engagement and faster development, playing a constructive role in maintaining global strategic stability and improving global governance. Zhang said that China-Russia military ties have in recent years advanced alongside broader bilateral relations, with significant progress in high-level exchanges and joint military exercises and training. China stands ready to work with Russia to fully implement the important consensus reached by the two heads of state, keep strengthening strategic communication, enhance mutual trust in the military field, improve cooperation mechanisms, and explore new areas of cooperation that reflect the characteristics of the times, in a bid to safeguard their respective sovereignty, security and development interests and uphold global and regional stability. Belousov said that, under the strategic guidance of the two heads of state, China-Russia strategic partnership of coordination in the new era has continued to deepen and reached an unprecedentedly high level, which is of vital importance to peace, stability and prosperity in both countries and the world, according to the MND. At present, the international security situation, particularly in the Asia-Pacific region, is complex and volatile. Russia appreciates and supports China’s active role in major international and regional affairs. Russia is willing to continue close coordination with China, strengthen strategic consultations, firmly support each other, expand practical cooperation in areas such as military education and scientific and technological innovation, and achieve further progress in relations between the two countries and their armed forces, Belousov said. Chinese and Russian naval vessels sail in formation towards the designated sea area during the maritime phase of the "Joint Sea-2026" exercise between China and Russia, July 10, 2026. Photo: Xinhua The “Joint Sea-2026” exercise between China and Russia concluded at a military port in Qingdao in East China’s Shandong Province on July 13. Launched on July 6 the joint exercise is the 12th in the series dating back to 2012. The joint naval exercises have become a key platform for China-Russia naval cooperation, strengthening their capabilities for combined maritime operations. Song Zhongping, a Chinese military affairs expert, told the Global Times on Tuesday that China and Russia maintain extensive military cooperation, spanning joint exercises and training, naval and air force exchanges, and counterterrorism efforts under the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) framework, reflecting the high level of ties between their armed forces. The new areas of China-Russia cooperation that reflect the characteristics of the times include opposing hegemony and power politics, as well as upholding a multipolar world order, Song said. Song added that China and Russia share broad common ground in opposing hegemony and power politics and upholding the post-World War II international order, making their cooperation important for regional and global peace.

item.title: China's resident-led renewal efforts give old neighborhoods new life
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-03 08:19:00
This photo taken on Aug. 11, 2025 shows a view of the renewed neighborhood Zhegong Xincun in Gongshu District of Hangzhou, capital of east China's Zhejiang Province. (Xinhua) Amid the ongoing urban renewal drive in China, residents in an east China neighborhood have spearheaded a new model by raising funds for rebuilding their dilapidated residential block. Unlike the government-led model that typically offers residents new apartments and cash compensation, this project saw its 548 homeowner households raise 499 million yuan (about 74.32 million U.S. dollars), more than 80 percent of the reconstruction bill, with the government covering the rest. The compound with 13 previously run-down buildings, known as Zhegong Xincun, sits in the downtown Gongshu District of Hangzhou, capital of the affluent Zhejiang Province. These six-story walk-ups were transformed into seven mid-rise buildings, surrounded by green spaces and shared facilities, in February last year. Hangzhou was an early adopter of this approach. It is among initiatives piloted across Chinese cities, from Harbin in northeast China's Heilongjiang Province to Shenzhen in south China's Guangdong Province, to avoid large-scale land acquisition and heavy investment from developers. Such pilot projects address long-standing hurdles for urban regeneration in China. Small scattered plots often deliver slim returns for commercial developers, and matching residents' compensation expectations has frequently stalled renewal plans, said Wu Songtao, professor at the School of Architecture and Design of Harbin Institute of Technology. According to a State Council executive meeting held in May, China is shifting from the stage of large-scale incremental expansion to a stage focused on improving the quality and efficiency of existing urban stock. "Instead of large-scale demolition, the goal now is to revitalize existing buildings, factories, neighborhoods and public spaces," said Zheng Degao, vice president of the China Academy of Urban Planning and Design. Zheng added that all beneficiaries, namely government, businesses and property owners alike, should share both the costs and the benefits. But translating this vision into practice was no easy task. Renewing old neighborhoods involves many interests and is prone to disputes, said Li Yin, an official with Gongshu District. Previous attempts to renew Zhegong Xincun all failed due to residents seeing only limited benefits and strains on public finances. Built in the 1980s and 1990s as faculty housing for Zhejiang University of Technology, the compound sits in a prime location in central Hangzhou, surrounded by shopping areas, metro stations and a large hospital. However, over the years, safety hazards mounted. Stiff windows were difficult to close, and building settlement warped door frames and locks, sometimes forcing residents to climb over walls to enter their homes. "The plaster crumbled at the slightest touch. We lived in fear every day," said a resident surnamed Yu. The university once carried out reinforcement work, but the effect was limited. Because the buildings continued to tilt and crack due to ongoing building settlement, such measures offered only temporary relief. A previous housing-relocation plan failed to win broad support. According to residents, a 2014 survey on demolition and reconstruction, and another attempt in 2018, both came to nothing. "The old idea was that the government should cover everything, from relocation to renovation," one resident said. "But as previous plans kept falling through, we realized we had to do it ourselves." This photo taken on Aug. 11, 2025 shows a view of the renewed neighborhood Zhegong Xincun in Gongshu District of Hangzhou, capital of east China's Zhejiang Province. (Xinhua) The turning point came in April 2023, when the subdistrict community office reached out to residents for their opinions on starting a resident-led renewal project. With support from local policies on renovating old urban neighborhoods, Gongshu District developed and adopted a resident-led renewal model for the compound. The initial stage of the renewal project was launched in mid-2022. The district set up a special task force to coordinate departments, study relevant policies and win public support via explanations. Local officials said that the harder part was reaching a consensus. "The core of the entire project lies in community engagement, shifting residents' mindset from being asked to renovate to wanting to renovate," Li said. A voluntary committee of 13 representatives was formed. After consulting all households, it submitted an application and entrusted local authorities to coordinate and initiate the renewal. By late August 2023, all but one of the compound's 548 homeowner households had signed agreements, bringing the signing rate to 99.82 percent, thus paving the way for the renewal plan to move forward. In May 2024, the last household came forward to sign before delivery. "This last resident later told me, 'I watched for a long time, and I could see the project is fair,'" Li said. Yu calculated that her original 76-square-meter apartment, plus an additional 19 square meters and a parking space, brought her total payment to nearly 980,000 yuan. "I originally bought the apartment for 1.51 million yuan. Even with this expense, my total cost remains below the market price, and I have more living space. I am also a beneficiary," she said. The project, though, has benefited from the community's demographics. Experts noted that although Zhegong Xincun is an aging community, its residents, mostly Zhejiang University of Technology faculty members and their families, are relatively better off, a factor that helped the project move forward. When the project was launched, the community also had a large elderly population, with 208 residents aged 80 or above and 36 aged 90 or above. Some feared a long construction period might keep them from returning, while others with children overseas faced the daunting task of relocating alone. To address these concerns, the working group provided comprehensive support. Ambulances were arranged to escort several residents over 90 on the moving day. Transitional housing was secured and rented to elderly residents, refurbished with age-friendly features such as shower seats and toilet grab bars. The compound was handed over last year, with about 70 percent of households having moved in, and they have begun renovating their new homes. The approach of Zhegong Xincun aligns with China's grand roadmap to advance urban renewal as the country endeavors to create safer, greener and more comfortable cities, while fostering new growth momentum. Under the urban renewal plan during the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-2030), China aims to renovate 500,000 units of dilapidated urban housing and 115,000 old urban residential communities. It supports resident-led renewal and on-site demolition and reconstruction of old housing, while exploring sustainable operation models. "This resident-led renewal model has opened a new path for urban renewal in China," said Xu Lin, a professor at Zhejiang University, noting that as China's urbanization enters a new phase, cities are no longer expanding through large-scale demolition and construction, but focusing on improving living conditions for residents. "At the end of the day, it's about giving people a better life," said Xu.
